MODULE_GOAL: Comfort with single-qubit states and visual representation.

LEARNING_OBJECTIVES: Write a single-qubit state in the form |ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩.
State and apply the normalization condition |α|² + |β|² = 1.
Identify the computational basis vectors |0⟩ and |1⟩ as column vectors.
Determine whether a given pair (α, β) represents a valid qubit state.
SUBTOPICS.CORE_EXPLANATION:
The state of a single qubit is fully described by a two-dimensional column vector of unit norm — that is, a vector whose entries, when squared in magnitude, sum to exactly 1. This vector is called the quantum state vector, and it holds all the information needed to describe the qubit, just as a single classical bit's value holds all the information needed to describe a classical binary variable. Any two-dimensional column vector of real or complex numbers with norm 1 is a valid quantum state for a qubit; concretely, a vector [α, β]^T represents a qubit state whenever α and β are complex numbers satisfying |α|² + |β|² = 1.

Two special vectors, [1, 0]^T and [0, 1]^T, are singled out because they correspond exactly to the two classical bit values 0 and 1. By standard convention, 0 ≡ [1, 0]^T and 1 ≡ [0, 1]^T, written |0⟩ and |1⟩ in Dirac notation. Together these two vectors form a basis for the qubit's vector space — meaning every other valid quantum state can be written as a weighted sum of them. Specifically, the general vector [x, y]^T can always be written as x|0⟩ + y|1⟩. This particular choice of basis is called the computational basis; although any rotation of these two vectors would work equally well as a basis, the computational basis is the one chosen by convention because it lines up with the classical 0/1 outcomes we eventually measure. Out of the infinitely many valid single-qubit state vectors, only |0⟩ and |1⟩ themselves correspond to definite classical bit values — every other valid vector represents a genuine superposition of the two.
SUBTOPICS.MATHEMATICAL_REPRESENTATION:
|ψ⟩ = α|0⟩ + β|1⟩ = [α, β]^T,  with  |α|² + |β|² = 1
Computational basis: |0⟩ = [1, 0]^T,  |1⟩ = [0, 1]^T
General decomposition: [x, y]^T = x|0⟩ + y|1⟩
SUBTOPICS.INTUITION_ANALOGY: Think of the qubit's state vector like a recipe that must always use exactly '100% of the ingredients' — no more, no less. α and β tell you how much of |0⟩-flavor and |1⟩-flavor go into the mix, but the squared amounts must always add up to a whole (1), the same way two tinted paints mixed in different proportions must still add up to one full can of paint.

LEARNING_OBJECTIVES: Define global phase as an overall factor e^(iφ) multiplying the entire state vector.
Explain why global phase has no effect on measurement probabilities.
Define relative phase as the phase difference between the α and β amplitudes.
Explain, at a conceptual level, why relative phase is physically meaningful (it affects interference and distinguishes otherwise similar-looking states).
SUBTOPICS.CORE_EXPLANATION:
Measurement outcomes for a qubit depend only on the squared magnitudes of its amplitudes: P(0) = |α|² and P(1) = |β|². Because of this, multiplying the entire state vector by an overall sign or, more generally, by a phase factor e^(iφ) (where φ is any real number) does not change either probability at all — negating both α and β, for instance, leaves |α|² and |β|² exactly the same. This kind of overall, whole-state multiplier is called a global phase, and it is considered physically unobservable: two state vectors that differ only by a global phase describe the exact same physical state, and no experiment can tell them apart.

Relative phase is a different, and physically meaningful, concept. It refers to the phase difference between the α and β amplitudes within a single state — for example, the states (1/√2)|0⟩ + (1/√2)|1⟩ and (1/√2)|0⟩ − (1/√2)|1⟩ have identical measurement probabilities in the computational basis (50/50 for each), yet they are genuinely different quantum states, because the relative sign (a relative phase of π) between the two amplitudes changes how the state behaves under further operations, such as passing through another gate, or how it interferes with itself. This distinction — global phase is invisible and irrelevant, while relative phase is real and observable through interference — is one of the more subtle but important ideas in single-qubit quantum mechanics, and it becomes especially visible once gates like the Hadamard (H) gate are applied to states that only differ by relative phase.
SUBTOPICS.MATHEMATICAL_REPRESENTATION:
Global phase: e^(iφ)(α|0⟩ + β|1⟩) describes the SAME physical state as α|0⟩ + β|1⟩, for any real φ
P(0), P(1) unchanged by global phase, since |e^(iφ) α|² = |α|² and |e^(iφ) β|² = |β|²
Relative phase example: |0⟩ + |1⟩ (relative phase 0) vs. |0⟩ − |1⟩ (relative phase π) — DIFFERENT physical states
SUBTOPICS.INTUITION_ANALOGY: Global phase is like rotating an entire clock face (numbers and all) by the same fixed amount — the relationships between the hands don't change, so it still tells the same time; no outside observer looking only at 'what time is it' can detect the rotation. Relative phase, on the other hand, is like changing the angle between the hour and minute hands themselves — that really does change what time the clock shows, and it's something you can actually observe and act on.

EXAMPLES.RESULT: Both states give P(0) = 0.5, P(1) = 0.5 — physically indistinguishable

EXAMPLES.DESCRIPTION: Relative phase distinguishes two states with identical basis-measurement probabilities
EXAMPLES.RESULT: Both give P(0) = P(1) = 0.5 when measured in the computational basis, but applying an H gate sends |+⟩ → |0⟩ and |−⟩ → |1⟩ — proving they were different states all along

COMMON_MISCONCEPTIONS: Global phase is NOT the same as relative phase — global phase multiplies the whole vector and is unobservable; relative phase is a difference between amplitudes and is observable.

Two states with identical measurement probabilities in the computational basis are not necessarily the same state — relative phase can still distinguish them under other operations or measurement bases.
'Unobservable' does not mean 'unimportant' in calculations — global phase can still matter for bookkeeping during multi-step derivations, it simply never affects final measurement statistics.

LEARNING_OBJECTIVES: Describe the Bloch sphere as a way of representing a single-qubit state as a point on (or in) a 3D sphere.
Identify the north and south poles of the Bloch sphere as |0⟩ and |1⟩ respectively.
Explain why the Bloch sphere works for single qubits but not directly for multi-qubit systems.
Qualitatively map a given single-qubit state to an approximate location on the Bloch sphere.
SUBTOPICS.CORE_EXPLANATION:
A single qubit's state vector is a two-dimensional complex vector, which is hard to visualize directly. The Bloch sphere solves this by giving a way to picture that same state as a point on the surface of an ordinary three-dimensional sphere, using a real-valued 3D vector (an arrow from the center of the sphere to a point on its surface) instead of two complex numbers. By convention, the north pole of the Bloch sphere represents the state |0⟩ and the south pole represents the state |1⟩; every other point on the sphere's surface represents some superposition of |0⟩ and |1⟩, with points along the equator representing equal-superposition states such as |+⟩ and |−⟩ that differ only in relative phase.

The value of this picture is that it turns quantum operations into intuitive geometric rotations: each valid transformation applied to a qubit corresponds to rotating the arrow about one of the sphere's axes. This makes it possible to reason about a sequence of operations as a sequence of physical rotations, which is a powerful and intuitive way to think about single-qubit quantum computation, even though translating this intuition into precise algorithm design still requires the underlying mathematics. One important limitation is that the Bloch sphere works only for a single qubit; for systems of two or more entangled qubits, the neat correspondence between quantum states and points on a 3D sphere breaks down, since multi-qubit states generally can't be captured by a small number of real-valued coordinates in the same simple way.
SUBTOPICS.MATHEMATICAL_REPRESENTATION:
General single-qubit state (up to global phase): |ψ⟩ = cos(θ/2)|0⟩ + e^(iφ) sin(θ/2)|1⟩
θ ∈ [0, π]: polar angle (θ=0 → north pole → |0⟩; θ=π → south pole → |1⟩)
φ ∈ [0, 2π): azimuthal angle, encodes the relative phase between α and β
Poles: |0⟩ at (θ=0), |1⟩ at (θ=π); equator (θ=π/2) contains equal-superposition states
SUBTOPICS.INTUITION_ANALOGY: Picture a globe: the North Pole is labeled |0⟩ and the South Pole is labeled |1⟩. A qubit in a 'pure' classical state sits exactly at one of the poles. As you move away from a pole toward the equator, the qubit becomes more and more an even mix of |0⟩ and |1⟩; the equator itself is 'home' to all the perfectly balanced 50/50 superpositions, which differ from each other only by their longitude — corresponding exactly to relative phase. Applying a quantum gate is like spinning the globe around some axis: the labels on the globe don't move, but the arrow pointing to your qubit's location does.

EXAMPLES.BLOCH_LOCATION: Equator, φ = 0 (points along +x axis by common convention)

VISUALIZATIONS: 3D Bloch sphere diagram with |0⟩ labeled at the north pole and |1⟩ at the south pole

COMMON_MISCONCEPTIONS: The Bloch sphere shows a *single* qubit's state; it does not directly generalize to multi-qubit or entangled systems.
Points on the Bloch sphere already account for global phase (which is discarded), so two vectors differing only by global phase map to the exact same point.

The 'inside' of the sphere is not used for pure states — valid pure single-qubit states always lie exactly on the surface (norm 1); points strictly inside represent mixed states, a more advanced topic.

LEARNING_OBJECTIVES: List the standard single-qubit gates: X, Y, Z, H, S, T and their matrices.
Describe each gate's effect as a rotation of the Bloch sphere arrow.
Predict how X, H, and Z transform a given basis or superposition state.
Distinguish Clifford gates (X, Y, Z, H, S) from the non-Clifford T gate.
SUBTOPICS.CORE_EXPLANATION:
Quantum computers process information by applying gates — unitary transformations — to qubits, and every single-qubit gate can be understood as some rotation of the Bloch sphere arrow. Single-qubit gates split into two families: Clifford gates and non-Clifford gates. The standard Clifford gates are the Pauli operators X, Y, and Z, together with the Hadamard gate H and the phase gate S (where S = T², i.e., applying T twice gives S). The only standard non-Clifford gate is the T gate (also called the π/8 gate). Together, the Clifford gates plus T form a set that can approximate any single-qubit unitary transformation, which is why they are often taught as the essential building blocks.

Geometrically: the Pauli X gate flips the qubit (it swaps |0⟩ and |1⟩) and corresponds to a 180° rotation about the Bloch sphere's x-axis. The Pauli Z gate leaves |0⟩ unchanged but flips the sign of |1⟩ (a relative-phase flip), corresponding to a 180° rotation about the z-axis; Y is a combined bit-and-phase flip, rotating 180° about the y-axis. The Hadamard gate H creates or removes superposition: it sends |0⟩ to the equal-superposition state |+⟩ and |1⟩ to |−⟩, corresponding to a 180° rotation about an axis diagonally between the x- and z-axes. The S gate applies a 90° phase rotation about the z-axis (multiplying the |1⟩ amplitude by i), and the T gate applies a smaller 45° phase rotation about the z-axis (multiplying the |1⟩ amplitude by e^(iπ/4)). More generally, continuous rotation gates R_x(θ), R_y(θ), and R_z(θ) rotate the Bloch arrow by an angle θ about the x, y, or z axis respectively, and any single-qubit unitary can be built from a sequence of such rotations.
SUBTOPICS.MATHEMATICAL_REPRESENTATION:
X = [[0,1],[1,0]]              (bit flip; 180° rotation about x-axis)
Y = [[0,-i],[i,0]]              (bit+phase flip; 180° rotation about y-axis)
Z = [[1,0],[0,-1]]              (phase flip; 180° rotation about z-axis)
H = (1/√2)[[1,1],[1,-1]]        (creates/removes superposition; 180° rotation about the (x+z)/√2 axis)
S = [[1,0],[0,i]] = T²          (90° phase rotation about z-axis)
T = [[1,0],[0,e^(iπ/4)]]        (45° phase rotation about z-axis; non-Clifford)
R_x(θ) = [[cos(θ/2), -i sin(θ/2)], [-i sin(θ/2), cos(θ/2)]]
R_y(θ) = [[cos(θ/2), -sin(θ/2)], [sin(θ/2), cos(θ/2)]]
R_z(θ) = [[e^(-iθ/2), 0], [0, e^(iθ/2)]]
SUBTOPICS.INTUITION_ANALOGY: If the Bloch sphere is a globe with |0⟩ at the North Pole and |1⟩ at the South Pole, then X is like flipping the globe upside down (pole swaps with pole) by spinning it 180° around an equatorial axis. Z is like giving the globe a half-twist around its own polar axis — the poles stay put, but anything on the equator ends up on the opposite side. H is the trickiest: it's like tipping the globe onto its side around a diagonal axis, so the North Pole ends up somewhere on the equator (superposition) and vice versa. S and T are gentle twists around the polar axis — S a quarter turn, T a smaller one-eighth turn — that leave the poles fixed but rotate anything already on the equator part-way around.

EXAMPLES.RESULT: |0⟩ → |+⟩; measurement now gives 0 or 1 with 50/50 probability
|1⟩ → −|1⟩; measurement probabilities are unchanged (still certainly 1), but the relative phase has flipped, which matters for later gates

EXAMPLES.DESCRIPTION: H gate applied to |+⟩ (H is self-inverse)
EXAMPLES.RESULT: |+⟩ → |0⟩ (H undoes itself: applying H twice returns the original state)

EXAMPLES.DESCRIPTION: Combining gates: H then Z then H (demonstrates X = HZH)
EXAMPLES.RESULT: |0⟩ → |1⟩, showing that the sequence H, Z, H has the same overall effect as a single X gate

VISUALIZATIONS: Bloch sphere animation: X gate rotating the arrow 180° about the x-axis, swapping poles
Bloch sphere animation: H gate rotating the arrow 180° about the diagonal (x+z)/√2 axis, sending |0⟩ to the equator
Bloch sphere animation: Z, S, and T gates shown as increasingly smaller rotations (180°, 90°, 45°) about the z-axis
Side-by-side matrix + Bloch-sphere-rotation view for each gate (X, Y, Z, H, S, T)
COMMON_MISCONCEPTIONS: The Z gate does not change the probability of measuring |1⟩ when starting from |1⟩ — it only changes the relative phase, which is invisible until further gates or interference are involved.
H is its own inverse (applying it twice returns the original state) — it is not a 'one-way' operation.
S and T are not the same gate: T is the more 'fundamental' non-Clifford building block, and S = T² (applying T twice equals one S).
